title: Shalya takes the reins
hook: Karna takes command, and asks for a king to hold his reins
carry: buddhi, discernment, should hold the reins

segments.voice: Yesterday: Drona, the teacher, fell, and your line was satyam vada: even a half-truth costs. Bhishma is down, and now Drona too. So who leads the Kauravas now?

A new commander needs a driver. In the Kaurava camp, Duryodhana turns to his friend Karna and gives him the army. Karna accepts, and then he says something honest. Arjuna has an advantage I don't, he tells Duryodhana, in effect: he has Krishna holding his reins. If I'm to face him, I need a charioteer who knows horses the way Krishna does. And Karna names the man: Shalya, king of Madra, the uncle of the Pandava twins, who ended up fighting on the Kaurava side.
screen: `KARNA TAKES COMMAND.` → `ARJUNA HAS KRISHNA.` → `I NEED SHALYA.`

segments.voice: Duryodhana goes to Shalya and asks, and Shalya is furious. In Ganguli's English, the king takes it as an insult: he, a crowned king, told to drive for Karna, who was raised in a charioteer's house. He nearly walks out of the camp. So Duryodhana talks him round, with an old story of the gods in which the creator Brahma himself drove the chariot for Shiva. Driving, in that story, is no shame. Shalya agrees, with one condition: he'll say whatever he likes to Karna's face. Karna accepts. Now the layer underneath. Before the war began, the epic tells us, Shalya promised Yudhishthira that if he ever drove for Karna against Arjuna, he would wear down Karna's courage with his words. So look at the two chariots. Arjuna's driver is Krishna, steadying him. Karna's driver is a voice in his ear, working for the other side. Hindus have an old picture for this, from the Katha Upanishad. Know the self as the rider, it says, and the body as the chariot. The senses are the horses, the mind is the reins, and buddhi, discernment, is the charioteer. When discernment drives, the horses run true. When it doesn't, the senses bolt like wild horses. Many teachers read the war's chariots through that picture: Arjuna gave his reins to Krishna; Karna handed his to a driver who was never truly his. And the picture leaves you with one old question: who is driving?
screen: `SHALYA TAKES OFFENSE` · `I WILL SAY WHAT I LIKE` · `A PROMISE TO THE OTHER SIDE` · then, large: `WHO IS DRIVING?`

segments.voice: Rest your hands on your knees, loosely, like reins held without pulling. Picture the Katha Upanishad's chariot: the senses are the horses, the mind the reins, discernment the driver. Breathing in, notice what's pulling hardest today: your phone, a worry, someone's voice. Breathing out, let discernment take the reins back, gently, with no yanking. If you pray, you can ask God to steady the driver; if not, just let the breath run slow and even.
Karna. The new commander of the Kauravas, who asks for a king to drive him, and gets a king who carries a promise to the other side.
Your line: buddhi, discernment, should hold the reins. Karna got a driver with a promise to the other side. Day eight hundred thirty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Hindus meet Karna's last battle through recitations and readings of the Mahabharata, retellings, regional theater and television serials; the Karna Parva, the epic's book named for him, tells this part of the war.
